item.title: Surviving Divorce: How to Thrive While Experiencing Loss
item.description:
Painful life experiences abound, and a good deal of them are connected with relationships. We are relational and social creatures, with the result that our relationships make up a large portion of what matters most in our lives.

When our relationships are healthy, that’s a good indicator that we’re flourishing. When things go awry in relationships, it affects overall well-being. Nonetheless, surviving divorce and flourishing when a marriage ends is possible.

The Complexities of Divorce

It would be a mistake to think that divorce is easy, especially when the marriage was marked by unhappiness and interminable struggles. Divorce can be and often is one of life’s most painful experiences, regardless of the circumstances.

When most people enter a marital union, they do so with hope and faith that they will be happy together for the rest of their lives. Ending such a relationship comes with layers of grief and confusion.

Working through divorce requires that you face the situation with honesty as well as healthy support that helps to anchor you through it all. There isn’t just one path that everyone who’s getting divorced takes. Every marriage is its own story, and the end of a marriage is also its own unique story.

When a divorce happens, it’s rarely the result of a single event. Often, there are many steps along the way that lead to the eventual breakdown of a marriage, to the point where a couple can’t see themselves together.

That process may take months or years, and it brings about many complex emotions like guilt, anger, grief, shame, and even relief. These emotions can appear at different times, and they touch nearly every part of a person’s life.

The most obvious change that a divorce brings is the change in relationship status, but that’s far from the only change. Divorce often brings other changes and concerns, such as needing to financially rearrange your life, adjusting your parenting responsibilities, and managing your living situation.

Another result of divorce is that it can stir up deep spiritual questions about forgiveness, your identity and sense of self in this new season, the Lord’s plan for your life, and your sense of security. It’s not just your relationship with your former spouse that changes; your relationships in the church, among friends, and with your extended family are also affected. There are many opinions and expectations to navigate.

The Challenges Divorce Brings to Your Well-being

Given the various complexities that divorce brings to your life, it isn’t surprising that it affects your well-being on several levels. For one thing, divorce can be stressful. There are financial costs involved, not to mention the logistical challenges that come with uncoupling. Stress often results in disrupted sleep, changes in appetite, and a negative impact on your overall health.

Emotionally, divorce is a source of grief, whether the relationship was good or not. Cherished dreams are being laid to rest, tears are shed for the years the locusts ate, and dealing with the heartache and pain you and your former spouse caused one another. There is fear of the unknown, and one may also have to grapple with a sense of failure.

Socially, divorce can change your landscape dramatically. Friendships, family connections, and church relationships can become strained or awkward. For their own reasons, the people in your life will choose sides, and that can have a devastating impact if it means losing friends and vital support at such a critical time.

Lastly, spiritually, divorce can leave you grappling with feelings of shame and guilt. You may begin to perceive yourself negatively and maintain unhealthy self-talk. Others experience a feeling of distance from the Lord, even in those situations where the decision was unavoidable.

Divorce can impact every aspect of your well-being, leaving you vulnerable to poor physical, emotional, mental, and spiritual health. If these challenges don’t get addressed, isolation, bitterness, and making use of unhealthy coping mechanisms are a true risk to keep a watchful eye on.

What to Avoid when Trying to Survive Divorce

Before launching into some healthy and effective ways to survive divorce, it may be helpful to take a detour and explore some common but unhealthy ways to try to survive a divorce.

It may be tempting, but avoid rushing into another relationship. Divorce can leave you feeling unworthy of love, and you may question your prospects or if you’ll even survive the world of dating post-divorce.

Whatever the case might be, take your time to heal and avoid trying to fill the void prematurely. Find your footing, work through your pain, and find joy before inviting another person into the deeper places of your heart and soul.

Another consideration is that you shouldn’t withdraw from the Lord or the church. Getting divorced can bring judgment from others, and your spiritual home may not feel safe any longer. You may feel shame or anger as you see how others around you are in light of this development, but you need to remain anchored in the Lord and among His people. That may mean finding a new spiritual home, but don’t withdraw from God or His people completely.

You should also avoid feeding revenge or bitterness. It can be tempting to narrate and re-narrate the ways your former spouse wronged you, or what should have happened. You can fuel anger, bitterness, and resentment as you dwell on what was or what should have been. Bitterness and the desire to get even may feel good, but they only serve to cloud your future and delay healing.

Do not ignore your physical and emotional needs. A relationship breakdown can take its toll on your body and mind. It’s not healthy to deny your grief or to ignore your needs at this (or any) time. These needs include the need to rest, so don’t overwork yourself. They also include the need for social interaction, to eat healthy food, expand your intellectual horizons, and connect meaningfully with God.

Lastly, you should also avoid making major decisions too quickly. Life may thrust some huge decisions upon you at this time, like needing to find a new home, changing jobs, or reentering the job market. Where it isn’t strictly necessary, however, avoid doing too much too soon. Give yourself the time you need to process what you’ve been through before making huge life changes.

Healthy Ways to Survive Divorce and Thrive

The Lord isn’t fond of divorce, given what marriage represents and the damage that divorce can cause (Malachi 2:16; Matthew 19:1-12; Ephesians 5:31-32). However, Scripture does speak to different circumstances for divorce (Matthew 19:9; 1 Corinthians 7:15), and life after divorce can be more than just survival. It is possible to thrive. Some healthy ways to work through a divorce and flourish include:

Allow yourself to grieve Recognize and acknowledge the loss fully. Different days and experiences may reveal new dimensions of loss, like the loss of companionship or support, or how your former spouse could bring out parts of you that no one else can.

Some people journal, while others prayerfully reflect on their marriage, and still others use art or creative expression to explore and release their emotions.

Stay connected to others We need community, especially in the dark times. When you’re isolated, it can lead to more rumination, slowing your healing process. Connect with friends, your Bible study group, or a ministry that helps you feel safe. Don’t disengage from the Lord either. Rather, take your heavy and uncomfortable feelings and thoughts to Him, because He cares about you (1 Peter 5:6-7).

Prioritize self-care and growth Don’t neglect your well-being in this season. Your emotional resilience can be bolstered by taking care of the ‘little’ things like good sleep, nutrition, regular exercise, and finding spaces of rest. As you go, seek the Lod and ask Him to show you new opportunities, places of growth, and ways to begin rebuilding and serving in line with His purposes for you.

Forgive and release The way to undo bitterness and stop it from gaining a foothold in your heart is to forgive them and yourself. This is not a way to excuse wrongs, but it releases you from bitterness and the need to get even. This is the only way for you to move forward with your life.

Seek support and counseling Divorce can leave open wounds and scars that need healing. By speaking with a trained and licensed counselor, you can find support and wise counsel during a challenging season of life. With help, you can emerge wiser, stronger, and more deeply rooted in your faith. Contact our reception team to get connected with a counselor who will walk with you on this journey.

item.title: Why the Signs of Bipolar Disorder in Women Are Missed During Major Life Changes
item.description:
When people think of bipolar disorder, they imagine mostly crazy mood swings, risky decisions, or extreme behavior. That’s true in many cases, but for many women, the signs can be harder to recognize, especially during big life changes.

The signs of bipolar disorder in women blend into the background of everyday stress, hormonal shifts, responsibilities, and the pressure to keep everything going. This is why mental health challenges like this go unnoticed, particularly during times like pregnancy, postpartum, menopause, or even during job changes or caregiving responsibilities.

Let’s look at why this happens, how it may happen, and what to do when it doesn’t feel quite right to check if bipolar disorder might be a factor.

Why Life Changes Make Things Less Clear

Throughout their lives, women go through major physical and emotional changes. These times naturally bring mood shifts, exhaustion, and irritability. Feeling tired, anxious, or emotionally sensitive after having a baby? That’s normal. Feeling irritable and foggy during menopause? Also normal.

But sometimes, these feelings are more intense than expected, or they come with bursts of energy, racing thoughts, or unexpected behavior.

That’s where things get confusing. Some signs of bipolar disorder in women are quite similar to normal hormonal changes, and they’re often brushed off. A woman might be told she’s just overwhelmed or going through a phase. And while those things may be true, they don’t explain everything.

Think about these examples:

  • A woman who just had a baby hasn’t slept in days. Suddenly, she feels full of energy in the middle of the night and starts reorganizing the house. A few days later, she crashes into sadness she can’t explain. This could actually be more than postpartum blues.
  • Another woman in her late forties starts feeling detached and flat. Then, out of nowhere, she feels jumpy, irritated, and full of restless energy. She may be experiencing a mixed episode.
  • Or a woman with a demanding career goes through phases where she works nonstop, filled with ideas and confidence, only to retreat completely the next week, feeling like she can’t get out of bed. She might be showing real signs of hypomania and depression.

In each case, the emotional ups and downs are real. But so is the possibility of bipolar disorder. And when the two collide, it’s easy to miss what’s really going on.

Why Functional Women Are Overlooked

One of the biggest reasons bipolar disorder goes unnoticed in women is that many of them are still functioning. They’re going to work, caring for kids, managing households, and caring for others. They may even seem more productive than usual during hypomanic phases. When they crash into depression, it’s chalked up to burnout or stress.

Just because someone is still getting things done doesn’t mean they’re feeling okay or mentally well. A few signs that are sometimes ignored in women who seem to be functioning well:

  • Feeling extremely motivated or wired for days, followed by a stretch of low energy or sadness
  • Making decisions on impulse, like sudden purchases, trips, or even quitting a job
  • Talking faster than usual or jumping from one idea to the next
  • Being emotionally sensitive or reactive, without a clear reason
  • Experiencing deep sadness that doesn’t respond to typical coping strategies
  • Having trouble sleeping during energetic phases and oversleeping during low ones

Many of these patterns can be subtle. They don’t always disrupt a woman’s ability to function, but they do affect her relationships, her sense of self, and her long-term mental health.

When Self-Doubt Gets in the Way

Many women live with their symptoms for years without seeking help, not because they’re fine, but because they second-guess themselves. They wonder if they’re just being too emotional, too dramatic, or not strong enough. They blame themselves for not keeping it together or for needing rest when others seem to manage just fine.

This self-doubt is one of the reasons the signs of bipolar disorder in women go unnoticed. Instead of speaking up, women push through. They adjust to the highs and lows, explain them away, and hope things will even out eventually. Some even feel guilty for bringing it up, especially if they’ve already been told it’s just stress or just hormones.

But guilt isn’t a diagnosis, and doubting yourself doesn’t mean you’re imagining things. You know when something feels off. Trusting that feeling is not weakness, it’s wisdom. Being open about your experience doesn’t make you difficult or dramatic. It makes you honest. And honesty is the first step toward support and answers.

In some cases, the signs of bipolar disorder in women are less obvious. They’re woven into personality, habits, or even coping strategies. If you’re wondering whether bipolar disorder might be part of your story, or someone else’s, there are a few less conventional clues to consider.

Other Clues That Don’t Always Get Noticed

  • You’ve been treated for anxiety or depression, but it doesn’t seem to fully explain what you feel. Maybe the medication helps a little, but not enough. Or maybe you’ve always felt like something’s missing from the diagnosis.
  • You feel like there are two versions of yourself. One is full of energy and ideas, the other is tired and disconnected. You swing between them, but you don’t know why.
  • Your moods seem tied to your cycle, seasons, or stress, but the emotional swings feel too strong to be typical. You feel like you’re on a rollercoaster you didn’t sign up for.
  • People say you’re intense or moody, but you’ve always felt like you’re just trying to keep it together. You may have learned to mask your symptoms or push through them, but that doesn’t mean they’re not affecting you.
  • You’ve done things on impulse, like spending sprees or sudden changes, that felt exciting in the moment but later left you confused or regretful.

All of these aren’t things everyone thinks of when they hear bipolar disorder, yet they’re part of what many women experience when living with it. This is especially true for bipolar II or mixed episodes, which are more common in women and harder to recognize.

If any of this sounds familiar, it’s worth exploring further. Bipolar disorder is treatable, but only if it’s properly diagnosed. Many women spend years being treated for depression or anxiety without realizing there’s a deeper pattern underneath it all. And because the signs of bipolar disorder in women aren’t that easy to pick out, it’s important to advocate for yourself, or for someone you love.

What You Can Do Next

  • Start keeping track of your moods, energy levels, and sleep. Even short notes can help spot patterns.
  • Don’t ignore symptoms just because you’re keeping up with daily life. Mental wellness isn’t only about functioning; it’s also about feeling like yourself.
  • Find a mental health professional who understands the signs of bipolar disorder in women.
  • Ask about things like bipolar II or rapid cycling. These are more common in women. They are more subtle but still serious.

If what you’ve read here feels familiar, don’t ignore it. The signs of bipolar disorder in women are real, even if they’ve been misunderstood or overlooked in your life until now. You don’t have to figure this out by yourself, and you don’t have to wait until things get worse to reach out.

Talking to someone who understands women’s mental health, especially during life changes like postpartum, menopause, or times of high stress, can bring a sense of clarity that’s been missing for years. The right support can help you make sense of your moods, your energy, and the parts of yourself that feel unpredictable or exhausting.

You can speak with a licensed Christian counselor who truly listens and understands what you’re facing. Call one of the numbers on your screen or browse the counselors listed on this site to find someone who fits your needs. Whether you’re ready to book a session today or just want to ask a few questions first, someone is here to help.

item.title: Long-Distance Relationship Tips for Couples Who Met Online
item.description:
Distance means very little to couples today. Since the pandemic, there has been an enormous spike in the popularity of online dating. It is estimated that one in ten couples met online in 2024, with people in their thirties and forties following the hordes of younger internet users looking for love online.

Although dating apps have become an ordinary way for couples to meet, virtually none of them provide long-distance relationship tips or even advice beyond generic safety warnings. Online dating not only provides opportunities for those looking to find love but also several obstacles, challenges, and risks.

There are a few important things you must consider if you find yourself pursuing a digital romance, particularly if you want your online relationship to work out. More than most, online relationships have an intense impact on our mental health. Communicating online with a love interest you have never met in person can be intense, exciting, and unusual. However, at some point, every digital couple must agree on what they want long-term.

Instant Connection with Online Dating

Online relationships tend to happen much faster than in-person dating. In a matter of clicks, you are in a private conversation getting to know someone in the safety of your own home while still being miles away from each other. The first stage of internet dating is often connecting like this in an app or on a platform, before choosing a more suitable chat app to use, preferably one with video calling capabilities.

One of the first long-distance relationship tips for online couples must be this: be wary of anyone unwilling to do a voice call or a video call.

People will give legitimate excuses for not wanting to do voice calls or video calls. They’re busy, or they’re in public. However, excuses like these only hold up one or two times. There is absolutely no future for the connection until you have seen or at least heard each other. This is especially true if your initial connection with someone on the internet feels promising and worth your time, and if they say they are interested too.

The Next Steps When Online Dating

Let’s say that you have matched with someone online, and sparks and butterflies are flying. Maybe you have spoken with them, seen them, and confirmed that they are who they say they are. What is next? This is a crucial stage for many online couples, because it determines the future of your connection.

You might have both stated what you are looking for on your profile on the app. That might be the main reason you swiped on each other in the first place. The second long-distance relationship tip for online couples is to establish what you are both looking for early in the relationship. Do this part on a video or voice call if possible.

Being online enables people to be selfish and flaky. It’s too easy to lead someone on, even after love-bombing them, only to disappear as soon as the connection leaves the flirting stage. You can save each other a lot of time and potential disappointment by establishing as early as possible what it is you are hoping for.

You don’t need to share your five-year plan, unless that’s something you both want to do. However, it is essential that you know if there is a possibility of meeting in person within the next few months, or else you will be investing in a potentially fruitless relationship.

There are many people who find themselves in intense, intimate, and even truly loving relationships in a matter of months after meeting online. Some people maintain these kinds of long-distance digital relationships for years. It sounds pointless and even torturous, but there is often a psychological reason for these kinds of connections.

These couples tell themselves that the reason they have never met and remained long-distance is due to logistics or practicalities. After more than a year, however, that excuse is merely a smokescreen. You can legitimately meet your future lover online, but the relationship cannot live unless you meet in person.

Similarly, a couple can be separated by distance for a season, but there is no future to it unless you have a mutual goal to be together again at some point. Too many couples who meet online settle for having a digital romance because it is safe and easy, and doesn’t require more than communication. Lasting relationships thrive on intentionality and planning. If you do not have a shared goal as a couple, you will not have a shared future.

The Best Long Distance Relationship Tips

You can say that you are in a long-distance relationship with someone you have met online if you have interacted over a voice or video call, established your shared hopes and intentions for the connection, and made a plan to at least meet in person within the next year. Even then, you might encounter some unpleasant surprises, but the same risk is true of relationships that begin any other way.

Once you share a common goal, there are some things you can do that will ensure the health of the relationship until you meet in person.

  • Don’t rely on texting alone: Schedule meaningful virtual dates regularly and have fun using other apps together. You can play regular one-on-one games online, watch movies and series together while you text each other, make and share music playlists, and take each other on video tours of places you visit. Long-distance relationships in the digital age should never feel static or dull.
  • Develop a rhythm with each other: A healthy connection with a long-distance loved one doesn’t come from constant communication. It comes from being consistent and intentional. You build trust with someone by showing up when you say you will and making them a priority in your life. Every relationship needs its little rhythms and rituals, like goodnight texts, video calls in the middle of the day, or weekly date nights online.
  • Continue to communicate your needs and thoughts: Life happens and tests even the strongest relationships. There will be nights when you can’t make the call you intended to, or even when you would rather process certain events alone. This is more than acceptable, provided you communicate your thoughts and feelings. Nothing affects a relationship more than overthinking and arriving at unhelpful conclusions.
  • Follow up on your individual and shared goals: In any relationship, you must be your partner’s biggest cheerleader and most constant truth-teller. If you have established a joint goal, keep each other accountable to it. As important, however, is encouraging each other towards personal goals. Long distance is no match for the couple who are united in their support for each other.

A Shared Future Together in Person

We live in a wonderful age where connection is possible despite distance and time zones. Digital dating is a solid stepping stone to a future you could only once dream of. When you find your person, do your best to connect with them in a better way than texting. Make it a goal and priority to overcome the obstacles keeping you apart, and be intentional and consistent until you do. One day, you will conquer the distance and enjoy the closeness you fostered while apart.

If you would like some personal support as you navigate the world of digital dating, or if you feel like you would benefit from more long-distance relationship tips, we recommend you find a counselor to talk to. You might find someone suitable from our online catalog of counselors, or our reception team can help. Either way, a counselor can help you navigate long-distance relationship tips and online dating.

item.title: What to Do If You Encounter Signs of Infidelity in Your Spouse
item.description:
No one would like to think that it could happen to them, but any marriage can fall prey to infidelity. Infidelity is one of the main reasons why couples get divorced, and still, some couples experience infidelity and manage to work through it without arriving at divorce. There are many reasons why infidelity occurs. They can be more complex than the stereotypical image of an unhappy couple who turn outside the relationship to have their needs met.

There are some signs to look out for that can suggest that infidelity is either taking place or will happen soon. No one wants to be blindsided. Being aware of these possible signs will help you potentially nip the issue in the bud, or it may help you initiate a necessary conversation to address concerns.

When it comes to something as complex as human behavior and infidelity, one needs to be careful about how they read signs. Signs can be misinterpreted, or they may be pointing to something else entirely. While trusting your instincts if you feel something is wrong is not a bad way to go, proceeding with caution and being careful about making unfounded accusations is also a wise course of action.

Weigh the signs judiciously, and create room for a conversation with your spouse to explain their behavior. Below are a few of the signs to look out for that may point to infidelity.

Some Classic Signs of Infidelity

When a person is having an affair, whether that affair is an exclusively emotional one, a purely physical one, or one that is physical with real affections involved, it affects and changes them. Some of those changes may be subtle, while others are drastic and easy to spot. Human beings are creatures of habit, and we settle into patterns of behavior.

When new patterns of behavior emerge, and they don’t have a cause you can easily identify, that should raise some questions. Some patterns of behavior would suggest an attraction outside the primary relationship, and you should be aware of these. To ensure judicious wisdom when evaluating these signs, some alternative readings will be offered that may be worth thinking through to ensure that you’ve eliminated other, possibly innocent interpretations.

Sudden Interest in Their Appearance

If a person who hasn’t been very concerned about how they look suddenly begins to spend time grooming themselves, getting in shape, buying new clothes, cologne/perfume, and underwear, that should raise some concerns.

Of course, people can spark an interest in these things for a variety of reasons. Some benign reasons include starting a new job with different standards of dress and appearance, a midlife crisis, or experiencing a significant event that transforms their outlook on life, such as the death of a friend or a health scare.

You know what’s going on in your spouse’s life. If none of the alternatives resonate, their sudden interest in their appearance may be because of a third party. That doesn’t mean an affair is happening, but it might be pointing to your spouse having an attraction toward someone else and wanting to impress them.

Suspicious Financial Activity

Infidelity often has financial implications. Buying gifts, booking hotel rooms, and extra gas from driving farther than usual are a few extra expenses that may be evident. There is often a financial trail when infidelity is happening.

If you find unexplained purchases on your credit card, a larger phone or gas bill than the norm, and other financial oddities, it’s good to ask some questions. Keep in mind that with realities such as gambling addiction, shady financial practices from your spouse may stem from another source entirely, other than having an affair.

Increased Desire for Privacy, Secretive Behavior

In most healthy relationships, there is openness and a willingness to be held accountable. That doesn’t mean there shouldn’t be boundaries in a relationship, as boundaries can promote the health of a relationship and the people in it. However, changes in behavior can indicate a problem.

Hiding their phone from view when you’re near, no longer using the family computer to do their work, taking calls outside the room, changing their cloud storage settings so their devices don’t sync with the family account, and generally shutting off a part of themselves are a few indications that can point to something such as infidelity taking place. Other things like porn addiction could also explain this behavior, but that, too, requires a conversation.

Decreased Sexual Interest

Unexplained changes in sexual behavior in the marriage can also point to infidelity, inasmuch as those needs might be getting met elsewhere. Libido can change due to mental health challenges such as depression and certain medications. Pressures in life can also lower one’s libido. If these are excluded, and what’s left doesn’t quite add up, it may be a sign of infidelity.

Compensatory Behavior

Sometimes people will act nicer to make up for a guilty conscience or to cover up any suspicions of inappropriate behavior. Unexpected gifts that aren’t part of the norm or attached to significant events such as birthdays or anniversaries are often part of that compensatory behavior.

A partner may become more attentive, patient, sweet, generous, or compassionate. If such behavior is out of the norm for your spouse, and it isn’t attached to any significant events in their life (such as a new or renewed relationship with the Lord), some questions may be warranted.

Becoming Uninvolved

Infidelity requires energy, whether physical, mental, or emotional. With their energy being poured into the affair, you may find that they don’t have energy for their primary relationship. They may begin checking out of the relationship.

This happens in various ways, such as not fighting with you anymore and indicating they don’t seem to care one way or another, staying at work longer, unexplained absences and trips away from home, and other unusual things. They may not have the energy to play with the kids as much as before or be willing to help as much around the house.

There are other possibilities for these behaviors. This emotional and physical detachment may be the result of depression in men, for instance. Still, it may also signal that their energy is being used elsewhere.

Inadequate Responses When Questioned About Their Behavior

If you approach your spouse with concerns, consider their response. If you bring up things you’ve seen and heard that make you think infidelity is taking place, and their only response is anger, that can point to something they are trying to hide. Similarly, if they try to gaslight you, that too could point to the truth of the matter.

Consider the Signs Carefully

People aren’t necessarily formulaic about how they conduct affairs. The presence or absence of any one sign doesn’t mean it’s conclusive that an affair is happening. A bunch of signs taken together is certainly more suggestive of what’s going on.

Looking Beyond the Signs

Unless there is something conclusive, such as you walking in on your spouse having an affair or coming across a conversation or texts that show that an affair (emotional or physical) is taking place, one has to rely on signs and hints. Whether it’s your gut or a strange occurrence that has you on alert, it’s important to think about what comes next.

Talk through it Having a conversation about whether something might be going on can be difficult. Accusations can have repercussions for your relationship, but it’s important to bring up concerns and talk through them thoroughly.

It may turn out that there’s something else entirely that’s going on. If it is an affair, you may want to find out the details of the affair: who the affair is/was with, its duration, whether there is affection shared between them, and so on.

If there is no affair, if what raised your concerns was linked to any boundaries (for instance, privacy and what was perceived as secretive behavior), your spouse may need to consider that their boundary may be causing distress. Talk about changes you can make together.

Consider seeking help Express your concerns empathetically and clearly, indicating the various things you’ve seen that have brought you to this place, and talk through how to possibly remedy them. Affairs happen for a variety of reasons. Talking with your spouse about what may have led them to have an affair may bring up many emotions and questions about your relationship.

Having this conversation under the guidance of a trained and licensed marriage therapist can help you explore and unpack these questions and emotions in a constructive and safe space. Infidelity doesn’t mean the end of your relationship. It is possible to work through the issues and emerge stronger on the other side.

To connect with a counselor who can help, reach out to someone on this site.

item.title: Night Terrors in Adults: Symptoms, Causes, and Treatment Options
item.description:
Night terrors in adults can be terrifying, especially to those witnessing their loved one during an episode. Nightmares are common and typically happen hours after someone falls asleep. However, night terrors occur during the non-REM sleep, around one to three hours after falling asleep.

Knowing the symptoms and causes of night terrors in adults can help you manage episodes and seek professional help when needed.

Symptoms of Night Terrors in Adults

Symptoms of night terrors in adults can leave one feeling emotionally drained, fatigued, and unstable. The good news is that night terrors tend only to last a few minutes. Once you are aware of the occurrence of night terrors, you can work on managing symptoms.

  • Sudden screaming – Waking up abruptly one to three hours after falling asleep and screaming is a typical sign of a night terror. You may not be aware of your actions, and the screaming may not fully wake you.
  • Thrashing and pushing – People with night terrors may thrash around in bed or push others away. You may wake to find your bed linens and pillows on the floor, or things knocked off the nightstand.
  • Violent behavior – Often, people with night terrors behave violently, as if moving through a nightmare. They may not be awake enough to be aware of others around them.
  • No memory in the morning – Unlike nightmares, you may not remember having a night terror. Others may tell you about it, or you may see the evidence in and around your bed, but have no memory or only a vague memory of the event.

If you feel that you may harm yourself or others during a night terror, seek help immediately.

Causes of Night Terrors in Adults

The causes of night terrors in adults can vary. Factors, including environmental factors, may play a role. A counselor can help you delve into the underlying cause of your sleep disruption and assist you in managing behaviors.

  • Trauma and PTSD – Unresolved trauma and Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD) can trigger night terrors. Many people find that therapy helps them through trauma disorders.
  • Anxiety – Anxiety and chronic stress can work as underlying factors while you try to rest and sleep. Your subconscious can wake you as your mind tries to process perceived danger.
  • Extreme Stress – Extreme stress can result in chronic inflammation in the body, which can disrupt sleep. The body’s stress response releases adrenaline and cortisol in the body. In a constant state, the body stays in fight-or-flight mode.
  • Depression – Depression can increase your risk of sleep deprivation, poor sleep quality, and disruptions. Studies show that nightmares may lead to a higher risk of suicidal thoughts or self-harm. The studies did not elaborate whether the subjects suffered from only nightmares or if night terrors were grouped into the category.
  • Alcohol or Drug Abuse – Alcohol and substance abuse raise your risk of developing night terrors.
  • Genetics and Family History – Genetics and family history play a role in your risk of experiencing night terrors. Also, age is a crucial factor. Night terrors may re-emerge if the person suffered from them as a child and is extremely stressed or is the victim of trauma.

A counselor can help you determine the factors behind your night terrors and create a mental health plan to assist you in overcoming them.

Treatment for Night Terrors

Treatments for night terrors can include lifestyle alternatives to lower stress and anxiety, combined with counseling to move past obstacles that may be hindering your progress. As with anything of value, results may not be instantaneous. However, over time, you should have fewer incidences of night terrors and be better equipped to handle them.

  • Counseling – Talk therapy and Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT) may help get to the root of the night terrors and help in changing thoughts and behaviors.
  • Scheduled Wakeup Times – To offset the beginning of a night terror, try scheduling a wake-up time to disrupt the pattern. This is a temporary solution, as you are disrupting sleep. However, because night terrors typically occur within the first three hours of sleep, you have a much better chance of breaking the pattern. Consult with a sleep specialist and your counselor about a long-term solution.
  • Stress Management – Most night terrors are brought on by extreme or chronic stress. Learning stress-management and relaxation techniques and adopting healthy lifestyle habits could help reduce the occurrence of night terrors.

Your counselor may have more suggestions for lifestyle tweaks that could reduce the frequency of night terrors.

Christian Counseling Can Help with Night Terrors in Adults

Are night terrors making it difficult to rest? Are you worried about hurting yourself or others during an episode? Contact our office today to speak with a Christian counselor about treatment options, including Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT). Night terrors in adults can be addressed with lifestyle alternatives and Christian counseling treatments. Contact us today to get started.

item.title: The Danger of Overstepping Boundaries and How to Find Support
item.description:
Boundaries are what keep us safe. They create a safe border around your life that aligns with what you believe and what is important to you. They also protect the particularly vulnerable areas and give others a clear understanding of how you expect to be treated.

Boundaries are clearly important and help to create structure and protection for you. When those emotional borders are breached, it can feel like a violation. You may feel violated when this happens. It can even open the door for manipulation, guilt, and frustration. These put a strain on your relationships. It can drain your resources like your finances and your energy. And when you don’t put a stop to it, it can cause you to be a target for others.

Understanding Boundaries

A boundary, by definition, is “something that indicates or fixes a limit or extent.” (Merriam-Webster Dictionary) In the context of personal boundaries, it’s a clear guide telling the world how you expect to be treated and how you will likewise treat others in return.

Boundaries tell others and, more importantly, remind you what you’re willing to give and what you’re not. These invisible fences protect your time, resources, energy, and even your emotional well-being. Without them, it’s easy to be swept away by the demands of others.

The reality is that boundaries make relationships healthier. They prevent awkward confrontations. They prevent resentment, and they ensure that both parties are being fairly treated. They create structure and allow relationships to grow without draining you.

Some may criticize your boundaries, saying they’re selfish. Those critics are usually the ones who want to push past your comfort zone for their own gain. Even with clearly set boundaries in place, not everyone will respect them.

Relationship Types

Most people agree that boundaries are important to set. But setting boundaries can be tricky, especially in relationships where there’s a perceived hierarchy, like a parent and child relationship or a boss and employee.

It’s common for one party to feel automatically subordinate, which makes it easy for the other person to take advantage of their position. If you’re the subordinate, you might feel guilty if you push back against things that violate your boundaries for fear of retaliation.

A child might find it difficult to say no to a parent, even if that child is an adult. In long-standing relationships, old patterns of obedience or people pleasing can make standing up for yourself feel impossible. If you’re an adult, you might find it difficult to say no to your parents, even if their requests are unreasonable. Younger children might feel like boundaries are punishments, but they’re tools that teach respect and structure.

At work, especially under a boss or supervisor, it’s easy to let your own time and energy be stretched too thin because you feel obligated or threatened into compliance. An employee might naturally surrender rights they shouldn’t out of fear of being fired.

Overstepping Boundaries

Overstepping happens when someone ignores or violates the lines that you’ve clearly drawn or when someone takes (or tries to take) more than you’re willing to give. If you haven’t been clear or decisive in communicating your boundaries, then the fault might land on you. It’s a sign that it’s time to be transparent and clear.

Most of these issues can be resolved with an honest conversation. But if someone oversteps a boundary that you’ve clearly laid or repeatedly pushes those limits, it’s likely their behavior is not a misunderstanding.

Overstepping boundaries is a sign of someone else’s neediness, not your failure. Read that again. Read it a dozen times if you need to. Because it’s the truth and it’s a fact that often gets clouded, forgotten, or manipulated.

When people don’t respect your boundaries, your generosity and kindness become a weapon. A weapon in the hands of those who are manipulating you can be dangerous. These manipulators employ guilt tactics and abuse your kindness, using the best part of you for their good and your detriment.

Repeated violations can lead to frustration and even resentment. They often create a cycle where you feel guilty for merely protecting yourself. But how do you protect yourself? Over time, this will undermine your self-esteem, may change the way you interact with people in the future, and will certainly damage your relationship with them.

When you start rearranging your life to manage someone else’s, you’re no longer operating out of a heart of love but from pressure. This isn’t loving for either one of you.

Spiritual Principle of Boundaries

God calls us to love others, but He doesn’t ask us to sacrifice our own well-being in the process. In Matthew 5:37, Jesus reminds us to let our yes be yes, and our no be no. God wants honesty in our interactions, and establishing boundaries is a way of thriving in the life that God has given you.

Well-meaning Christians often confuse the idea of setting boundaries with being selfish. They believe that being Christ-like is synonymous with being endlessly available and self-sacrificing. Of course, the idea of dying to self is a solid Christian principle, so it’s no wonder that there is confusion. But dying to self refers to surrendering sin and selfish ambition, not healthy boundaries that safeguard the life God entrusted to you.

Christ didn’t model boundary-less living. Jesus himself stepped away from crowds to rest. He withdrew to pray. He said no to certain demands so He could say yes to the mission the Father gave Him. Even Jesus, who was perfectly loving, did not allow people to dictate His time or derail His purpose.

God never intended for you to live exhausted, either. He doesn’t want you to be resentful or drained dry. Psalm 121 reminds us that God watches over our comings and goings. He cares about your daily life, not just the big Instagram-worthy events. You can do this in your day-to-day life by protecting your peace, health, and time. This is a form of stewardship that honors God.

Therapy for Help with Boundaries

Psychology echoes the Bible’s idea of boundaries. Therapists explain that boundaries are necessary for emotional safety and help you maintain a balanced life. When you don’t set or enforce them, you expose yourself to unnecessary stress and can burden yourself with more responsibility than necessary. Those burdens can cause a myriad of negative consequences.

If you have a difficult time creating, communicating, and enforcing boundaries, seek professional help from a licensed therapist. Your therapist can walk you through the steps of deciding how you want to be treated by the people in your life. They can also help you learn how to communicate those boundaries effectively and how to enforce them.

Therapists can also help you recognize when your boundaries have been violated and give you practical and reasonable responses to employ in those circumstances. You can find support in these delicate situations that helps you recognize problem areas and learn new ways to move forward.

Starting with a therapist doesn’t need to be intimidating. You can connect with a Christian therapist who will share the same spiritual foundation discussed in this article. That will help you start from a place of shared purpose and understanding. It will also give you a model for how to live life with healthy, Godly boundaries.

You can reach out to a therapist near you or someone on this site. Therapy can be in person or virtual, offering an array of options so it fits into your life. You don’t have to continue living by other people’s needs. You can learn to create and maintain boundaries that support you.

Call or fill out the contact form on this site to learn more about how to meet with a Christian therapist who can help.

item.title: Beyond Tired and Into Emotional Exhaustion
item.description:
Have you had those moments where you feel depleted? You feel worn out, beyond tired, in a way that sleep doesn’t fix. At some point, ordinary fatigue crossed over into something else. You find yourself operating on autopilot through days that blur together and going through motions that used to feel meaningful, but now feel heavy.

This could be emotional exhaustion. It’s real, and it doesn’t announce itself with clear warnings. It often builds up quietly in the background until one day you realize you’ve been running on empty for quite some time.

The weight of this fatigue accumulates, and unless you’ve experienced it before, you don’t know how to understand it. You manage your responsibilities and show up where you need to be. Everything might look fine from the outside. Deep down, however, you know something has shifted in the energy you once had for people and activities. The energy you once had has been drained away.

What once helped you bounce back from difficult days has worn thin, and there is an unspoken pressure to keep functioning as though nothing has changed. This gap between what you’re doing and how you’re expected to present yourself leaves you feeling isolated and exhausted.

“Come to me, all who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest. Take my yoke upon you, and learn from me, for I am gentle and lowly in heart, and you will find rest for your souls. For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light.” – Matthew 11:28-30, ESV

When Stress Becomes Emotional Exhaustion

It’s no secret that stress is part of life. We all experience difficult seasons when demands are high, and challenges pile up. This is the result of doing things beyond our capacity for an extended period. Chronic unmanaged stress fundamentally changes how your brain and body function. You’re not just dealing with temporary pressure; you are dealing with a system that has been overworked to the point that it can no longer regulate effectively.

The reasons for exhaustion vary from person to person. It can be work-related, stemming from demanding jobs, toxic environments, and the constant pressure of high-stakes responsibilities. For some, it can develop from caring for aging parents or children with special needs. Most often, a significant life transition, such as divorce, loss, or relocation, can trigger it. Even financial strain, relationship conflicts, and health challenges can create emotional exhaustion.

For most people, it is not one overwhelming situation but an accumulation of multiple stressors that seem manageable when taken individually but together become crushing. Christian counselors are trained to work with people who can’t identify one single cause because the exhaustion has built up from many sources over time.

Recognizing the Signs of Emotional Exhaustion

Every day across every area of life, symptoms appear that you may not immediately connect to emotional exhaustion. You may notice that your concentration is lacking, and tasks that used to take twenty minutes are now stretching into hours because your mind keeps wandering. It may seem that your memory is unreliable, and you’re forgetting appointments, conversations, and commitments.

Another possibility is difficulty with decisions. Decision-making can become overwhelming and frustrating as brain fog settles in and refuses to lift. These are not signs of weakness or incompetence. They’re indicators that your cognitive resources have been depleted.

Emotionally, the changes can be staggering. You may find that you’re more irritable than usual, and you snap at people over minor frustrations. You may also notice that anxiety symptoms have increased. The optimism you once had shifts to cynicism or hopelessness as you lose interest in activities that once brought joy. Often, motivation is no longer apparent, and you feel apathetic about things that previously mattered.

Some individuals have described this as feeling numb and disconnected, as if they’re moving through life removed from their own experiences. Christian counselors are quick to recognize patterns of burnout like this. Guilt can also accompany these feelings, adding another layer of difficulty. This leaves you wondering why you can’t push through or why everyone else seems to be managing life better.

The Physical Toll Nobody Talks About

Emotional exhaustion isn’t contained to your mind and emotions. Emotional exhaustion can manifest in ways that cannot be ignored indefinitely. Frequent headaches can appear, and sleep patterns deteriorate, leaving you exhausted but unable to rest properly. You may also experience digestive system issues, chest pain, heart palpitations, and difficulty breathing.

Some people may notice they are catching every illness that comes because their immune systems are being affected. The body keeps an accurate record of stress even when you try to convince yourself that you’re managing fine.

Prolonged emotional stress contributes to severe health conditions, affecting cardiovascular health, immune function, and metabolic processes. The physical symptoms create their own stress cycle.

When you’re too exhausted to exercise and prepare meals, it affects the nutrition your body receives. When you are sleep-deprived, everything emotional seems intensified. The illness and the pain can add to your stress load, leading to a further depletion of your capacity to cope.

If you’re in a demanding career or a caregiving role, the physical toll can reach dangerous levels. If you’re operating equipment or making important decisions for vulnerable people while your own system is breaking down, this can cause not only injury to yourself but also to those you’re caring for. It is vital to identify the pattern, recognize that pushing through is unsustainable, and understand that your body is sending signals that need attention.

Beloved, I pray that all may go well with you and that you may be in good health, as it goes well with your soul. – 3 John 1:2, ESV

Finding a Way Through Emotional Exhaustion

Emotional exhaustion isn’t something you recover from overnight. It requires paying attention to both the sources of the stress and your capacity to manage them. The first step involves an honest assessment of what is causing the depletion. Then you need to be intentional about reducing or eliminating stressors that can be removed.

For the stressors that you can’t change, you learn to navigate differently. It is essential to understand how to distinguish between the stressors so that you’re not trying to alter unchangeable situations and waste precious energy.

It’s acceptable to start small with practical changes. This can be done by establishing boundaries around your time and energy, even when it feels uncomfortable. There may be times when you need to decline a request. By doing so, you can build actual rest rather than viewing every available moment as a chance to be productive. This means learning to prioritize sleep, nutrition, and physical activity, all necessary elements for healthy functioning.

The adjustment sounds simple, but during emotional exhaustion, it can feel nearly impossible. Christian counselors understand the importance of starting where you are, rather than waiting until you have the energy for dramatic changes. Small, consistent choices lead to lasting changes over time.

Finding support makes a significant difference for many people who are working through emotional exhaustion. Therapy can provide a structured space to process what is causing the overwhelming fatigue, help you identify patterns that keep you stuck, and give you a way to develop sustainable strategies for managing stress.

Acknowledging you need help is nothing to be ashamed of; it often marks the turning point between continuing to struggle and beginning actual recovery. Connecting with others who understand helps counter the isolation that emotional exhaustion creates. Prayer, Scripture, and spiritual community provide grounding when everything else feels unstable.

God is our refuge and strength, a very present help in trouble. – Psalm 46:1, ESV

Find support

You don’t have to accept living in a state of emotional exhaustion as normal. This depletion you’re experiencing is real; it deserves acknowledgment and a response. Your body and mind are sending clear signals that it’s time to get help for this exhaustion.

You can heal from emotional exhaustion by acknowledging where you are and that you need help. Your local Christian counseling services can provide the help you need to recover from emotional exhaustion. Connect with someone on this site to get started.

item.title: What To Do Before Getting Married
item.description:
Saying “I do” is only the first step before getting married. You may not think about everything else that you need to do before the actual wedding, which doesn’t have anything to do with the date. Planning for marriage is more important than planning for the wedding. The wedding will last one day, but the marriage will, hopefully, last decades.

Before getting married, consider the following tasks.

Christian Premarital Counseling

Christian premarital counseling combines biblical principles and a faith-based lens with proven psychological methods to strengthen relationships. Using Jesus as the cornerstone, you can expect your sessions to lean toward understanding, love, forgiveness, and grace. You will learn the Bible’s viewpoint on subjects such as parenting, finances, living together, and more.

Christian premarital counseling before getting married also helps to draw you closer to Christ. You want to grow together spiritually and start your marriage off strong.

Keep your relationship strong

Being honest, fair, loyal, and faithful will keep your relationship strong, but it is easy to lose ground with more adult responsibilities. Prioritizing your relationship will always be a critical component of your marriage. If you feel like you or your significant other is losing sight of that, pause to take stock together about what can change.

As your family grows, parents age and need to be cared for, careers blossom, and other responsibilities crowd your life. Take the time to put each other first. No person or career should come between a husband and wife. Care for your family, but leave space open for your spouse.

Be a listening ear

Everyone needs to vent now and again. Stressful jobs, children’s behavior, teen angst, in-law drama – whatever the issue, be willing to listen to your significant other. Yours should be a willing and patient ear for them to unburden themselves, and they should be yours. Ask questions and show that you have an interest in their day.

When it comes to arguments between the two of you, extend grace and forgiveness, and be ready to find solutions that may require bending for both parties. Listen to your partner’s side and consider it before making a rash decision, and ask them to do the same.

Vow to work it out before getting married

Before getting married, vow to work it out no matter the odds. Obstacles will come against your marriage. Remember, “Your enemy the devil prowls around like a roaring lion looking for someone to devour.” (1 Peter 5:8, NIV) Temptations will come along, but if you follow Christ and vow to keep your marriage alive and strong, you can beat anything that aims to destroy your marriage.

Spiritual warfare includes attacks on marriage and family. When it seems like there is nothing left, commit to standing with each other against the world.

Discuss finances and living arrangements

It’s a good idea to discuss finances and living arrangements before getting married. Find out what your combined income will be, the amount of debt, and how you will manage checking, savings, investments, and retirement plans. Household budgets and living arrangements should also be created, so that you have a general idea of what you will need to live within your means.

If you and your significant other are unsure about managing finances, consult a financial advisor. Financial literacy is imperative in today’s technological world. You need to know how to budget and prepare for emergencies.

Get on the same page about children

Have you discussed children yet? Do you both want children? Sit down with your partner and discuss each other’s childhoods and what you want for your own children. Discuss how you want to handle birth control, spacing of births, discipline, and parenting. You don’t need to have all the answers yet, and you won’t until you become parents, but this will give you a general idea.

“Walking in the Wind”, Courtesy of Erik Mclean, Unsplash.com, CC0 License; If this marriage creates a blended family because children are already in the picture, discuss how you will handle new stepparenting roles, rules, boundaries, discipline, and quality time with each child. Blended families have their own issues that can cause problems in a new marriage.

Prioritizing your relationship is critical in a blended family. Children need security and routine, and you may not have those in place if you don’t plan accordingly before getting married.

Set boundaries with extended family

No matter how enamored you are with your significant other, when you marry them, you marry into their family. In-laws and extended family can create drama that can spill over into your marriage. Discuss with your partner what you want for your marriage and what boundaries the two of you need to set when it comes to family.

Make sure that you both agree on these new boundaries and discuss them with your family. If someone becomes offended by your new rules, explain that the two of you want to start your marriage off on a strong foundation and build your relationship, and that you ask that they respect your wishes.

Determine household chores

Household chores can be a sore spot for some couples. Often, the way a person perceives their role in chores falls on what they saw their role models doing during childhood. For example, if your husband’s mother did all the cooking and cleaning, then he may not realize that you want him to assume some responsibility.

Discuss your work schedules and obligations, and decide who will do what household chores, including laundry and property maintenance. If you cannot agree, consider hiring a house cleaner to come in once or twice a week or speak to a counselor to help you develop a fair plan.

Host a celebration that brings both families together

It is a good idea to introduce the families of the bride and groom before getting married. This gives everyone a chance to get to know one another. You could host a family get-together, picnic, or holiday feast.

Some couples use this time to announce their engagement and host games where in-laws must work together. You want to build a relationship with your in-laws, but don’t feel upset if there is a personality clash. People are only human after all. Just demand respect and peace from both sides.

Discuss your shared and individual vision for the future

You should be able to support your significant other in their goals while working toward your own. Discuss your individual and shared goals for the future. Will you both be content living in a specific area or city? Will your education be misaligned with your spouse’s career? Try to develop a shared vision.

If your goals seem to run contrary, not all is lost. Consult with a counselor to find a resolution. There will be times when one of you will need to make concessions for the other to make things better for both of you. It’s not about outsmarting or getting your way. It’s about building a future where both of you will benefit.

Doing what you can before getting married will lay a foundation that will last for years. Some of these conversations with your significant other may feel awkward and vulnerable, but these challenges will make you stronger. If you can’t be awkward and vulnerable with your soon-to-be spouse, you may need to spend a little more time with them.

Work together and voice your concerns and hopes. Share your vision of the future and listen to your significant other’s goals and dreams. Hold one another up even when things get hard.

Next Steps

If premarital counseling sounds like something you would like to try before getting married, call our office today to schedule a session. A Christian counselor specializing in premarital and marriage counseling will give you a call. You can choose to hold a session in-person at our local center or virtually. Call today to speak to a representative to get started.

item.title: Recovering from an Emotionally Abusive Relationship
item.description:
A healthy relationship provides you with a foundation and support system to help you flourish as an individual. When relationships are good, they have the potential to help you become the best version of yourself. The converse is also true; an unhealthy relationship can break you, leaving you unable to function at your best, or sometimes even at all. Being able to discern between healthy and unhealthy relationships is a crucial life skill.

For a variety of reasons, a person can be oblivious to what makes a relationship good or unhealthy. Life experiences can shape your expectations and dull your sensitivity to unhealthy behaviors. One of the steps to overcome these unhealthy relationship patterns is to see them clearly for what they are, to begin undoing them.

What An Emotionally Abusive Relationship Looks Like

When someone emotionally abuses you, what that means is they have failed to treat you with the dignity, love, and respect that you deserve as a fellow human being. It’s not just that they’ve neglected treating you in this way, but they’ve done and said things that are contrary to that dignity, respect, and what love demands. In other words, emotional abuse is not just the absence of some things, but the presence of harmful words, actions, and attitudes.

You’d think it would be easy to tell if you’re in an abusive relationship, but things aren’t always that simple. One reason for this is that emotional abuse tends to break you down, and that includes your perceptions and judgment. That means that other people might see what’s happening, but you might not see it or find ways to justify it. This can be baffling to outsiders.

As you try to identify the emotionally abusive traits in your relationship, it helps to recognize these traits, as well as to pay attention to how you feel. If, for instance, you’re constantly feeling anxious, fearful, depressed, trapped in the relationship, or if you are questioning your memory or sanity, or you’re walking on eggshells around your partner, that could all point to an emotionally abusive relationship.

Some of the signs of emotional abuse to keep an eye out for include:

Isolation and control You’re isolated from family, friends, and other loved ones, and you’re forced to rely on your partner for emotional support and social interaction. They try to control your interactions with others, your actions, or your decisions.

As a part of control, your partner may also engage in excessive monitoring, whether in person or through social media, phone calls, and text messages, to ensure you’re acting or behaving in the way they want.

Manipulation and gaslighting An emotionally abusive partner may try to use shame, guilt, or fear to influence your actions or interactions with others. They may also deny the truth, twist facts, or place false blame, with the result that it makes you doubt your memory, sanity, or perceptions. This is known as gaslighting.

Manipulation can take place in other ways, including through mood swings. When your loved one has unpredictable mood swings, alternating between being aggressive and affectionate, for instance, that can also function to manipulate you and your reactions. It also creates an unstable home situation that doesn’t feel safe.

Threats and intimidation Instead of feeling like a safe place, an emotionally abusive relationship feels unsafe. One reason for this is that your loved one makes threats, whether direct or implied, that they will harm themselves, you, or a loved one. Such threats are often leveraged to manipulate your decisions or actions.

Constant criticism and belittling None of us is perfect (Romans 3:23), but if you find yourself being frequently demeaned or criticized, especially over minor or trivial issues, that could point to emotional abuse in the relationship. If a loved one engages in behaviors that dismiss or undermine your ideas, thoughts, or achievements, leading you to question your intelligence or abilities, that could also signal emotional abuse.

Possessiveness and jealousy It’s normal to cherish the bond you and your loved one have and to be protective of it, but that’s distinct from having an excessive level of jealousy or possessiveness. The latter leads to unhealthy behaviors like controlling and monitoring, and the unwillingness to allow one’s partner to flourish and have independence or autonomy.

Emotional blackmail When someone uses your emotions against you to get what they want, that’s blackmail. This can happen in several ways, including threatening to end the relationship if you don’t comply, consistently blaming you for problems in the relationship, or giving you the silent treatment and withholding affection as a way to punish or to control you.

Disregard for personal boundaries Each person has their own limits and things they’re comfortable with. If your boundaries and feelings are disregarded when they’ve been clearly communicated, that’s also a sign of emotional abuse.

One of the challenges of emotional abuse is that it can leave you feeling uncertain, unsure of your position, and even questioning your reality. That’s a reason why getting an outside perspective is so important. Talking with trusted and wise friends, relatives, or a counselor can provide you with much-needed perspective on the relationship.

The Effects of An Emotionally Abusive Relationship

An emotionally abusive relationship can do a lot of damage to a person. Being constantly criticized or belittled can leave you feeling incapable and helpless. It knocks your confidence and sense of self-worth. You’re also left with a diminished ability to trust your own judgment, making it harder to make decisions or express your opinion. You might even feel confused about your thoughts and feelings.

Experiencing emotional abuse can cause stress, emotional, and mental turmoil. Those struggles can contribute to developing and worsening mental health problems like depression and anxiety. Emotional abuse can also worsen your well-being by isolating you, which cuts you off from your support network. Lastly, it can also result in health issues like disrupted sleep, headaches, and problems with your digestion.

Recovering from an Emotionally Abusive Relationship

When you’ve been emotionally abused, that doesn’t have to define who you are or shape your everyday reality. It’s possible to overcome the effects that emotional abuse has on you. The first step is to recognize and acknowledge that you’re in an emotionally abusive relationship. If you have a gut feeling that things aren’t right, don’t ignore that. Take the necessary next steps to address the situation, including educating yourself about emotional abuse.

You can carve out and allow yourself room to grieve, not only the relationship and whatever hopes you had for it, but also for your loss of safety and the damage the relationship caused you. Taking care of yourself should be a priority, and that includes hobbies that bring you joy, and activities like exercise that nurture your well-being. Whether it’s running, swimming, roller-skating, or gardening, do what helps you relieve stress and elevate your mood.

Recovering from emotional abuse also requires taking steps to rebuild your self-esteem. Being constantly criticized can leave you with a running commentary in your mind, and negative self-talk becomes a feature. Learn to pause, speak compassionately to yourself, and challenge the negative thoughts running through your mind. Pray over your thoughts, replacing those negative thoughts with words from Scripture.

Rebuilding your self-esteem may also involve setting healthy boundaries to curb further abuse and to give yourself space to do the kinds of things that help you regain confidence. For instance, learning a new skill, enrolling for a class, or completing a project can help you rediscover and reconnect with your gifts and abilities.

Other steps you can take to recover from an emotionally abusive relationship include creating new routines that help you to be more independent and self-sufficient. You don’t have to do this alone; seek support from trusted loved ones. Having someone with whom you can share your experiences can bring emotional relief and play an important role in coping. There are also support groups and online forums where you can meet others on a similar journey.

If your partner or spouse doesn’t want to make any changes, it could require you to make the hard decision to leave the relationship. It’s important to develop a safety plan so that you can leave safely. This may involve speaking with a trusted loved one or an organization that helps survivors of emotional abuse. The plan may require having important documents ready, a safe place to stay, financial resources, and a support network.

You should also seek professional help and support in the form of a counselor or therapist with training in addressing emotional abuse and recovery. Your counselor can help you process your thoughts and emotions, and they can walk with you to develop personalized coping mechanisms and strategies to heal and begin rebuilding your life.

To learn more and schedule an appointment with me or one of the other counselors in our online directory, contact our office today.
